While age varies (28, 48, 53), the majority of these individuals are in the working-age range (28–53), which is not inherently predictive of income level. The occupation varies (Craft-repair, Sales, Other-service), but all are common in lower-to-mid income brackets. The shared marital status and education level are statistically associated with stable employment, yet they do not strongly distinguish income class. Notably, workclass (Local-gov, Private, Private) shows only minor variation and does not clearly indicate bias. These shared features are semantically plausible in the context of income prediction, but their uniformity across misclassified instances suggests that the model may have learned spurious correlations—such as the assumption that being married and having a high school education leads to higher income—rather than capturing true income determinants. This indicates possible spuriousness due to data selection bias or overfitting to demographic patterns.
